title: JS first-class functions and EventTarget
hook: If you think in Node callbacks, map them onto delegates and EventTarget — do not say C# has first-class functions the way JavaScript does.

sections.heading: Functions as values, with a type system that survives
sections.prose: In JavaScript every function is an object. You pass it, return it, and stash it on a map without declaring a type. In C#, a method is not a value until you convert it to a delegate (or to an expression tree). The conversion is typed: parameter list and return type must match, with limited variance. That is why RabbitMQ middleware in C# is IList<Func<Message, CancellationToken, Task>> rather than an untyped array of callbacks. TypeScript’s (msg: Message) => Promise<void> is a close story at compile time and then disappears. The CLR still knows the delegate type at run time.

snippets.label: JS callback list versus C# multicast
snippets.explanation: This is multicast you built yourself. C#’s delegate type plus event add/remove is that pattern with CLR-checked signatures.

snippets.label: The same pipeline as typed Func values
snippets.explanation: Each step is a first-class value only after it is a Func. Method groups convert when the target type is known.

sections.heading: EventTarget compared with event
sections.prose: DOM and Node EventTarget: addEventListener(type, fn), removeEventListener(type, fn) with the same function reference, capture/once options, and a string event name. C# events are members, not a stringly-typed map. There is no built-in once; you unsubscribe yourself. There is no capture phase. Both systems leak if a long-lived emitter holds a short-lived listener. Both fail to unsubscribe if you pass a new function with the same source text. When an interviewer asks for a JS analogy, say EventTarget plus function values, then name the differences: typing, multicast exception behavior, and no runtime event-name registry on a typical C# type.

snippets.label: EventTarget must keep the same function reference
snippets.explanation: AbortSignal is the modern JS unsubscribe story. C# uses -= or disposing the publisher. Neither is garbage-collected automatically just because the listener went out of scope if the emitter still references it.

interviewTakeaways: JS functions are objects; C# methods become objects only as delegates.
EventTarget is the closest JS analogue to C# events; event names are strings in JS and members in C#.
Same-reference unsubscribe is required in both languages.
TypeScript function types erase; C# delegate types do not.
commonPitfalls: Saying C# has first-class functions without mentioning the delegate type.
Comparing event to Node EventEmitter’s string names without noting the typed member.
Assuming removeEventListener('message', () => {}) works — it does not, for the same reason -= new lambda fails.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Pass, return, and store functions freely. C# stores Func/Action/custom delegates instead of raw method tokens.
addEventListener/removeEventListener with identical references; AbortSignal for lifetime. Map this to event += / -= and IDisposable.
